title: Natural Resources and Where They Are Found
summary: What natural resources are, why they are spread unevenly around the world, and why some countries have more of certain resources than others.
poll: It is fair that some countries have more natural resources than others.

versions.title: Gifts from the Earth
versions.text:
The Earth gives us many things we use. These are called resources. Oil is one. Water is one too.

Rock can hold oil deep down. Some rock holds a mineral too. A mineral is a hard thing found in rock. Gold is a mineral. Iron is one too.

Not every land has the same things. Some land has lots of oil. Some land has none. Some land has lots of water. Some land is dry.

Why is this so? It is about the land itself. Hot, wet land can grow a forest. Dry land can not. Old rock deep down can trap oil. New rock may not.

So one land may have lots of oil but little water. A far-off land may have lots of water but no oil. That is why we trade.

Not every land on Earth has the same resources. Some land has lots of oil under it. Other land has none at all. Some land gets lots of rain and water. Other land stays dry most of the year.

So one country may have lots of oil but little water. A country far away may have lots of water but no oil at all. This is one reason why countries trade with each other.

versions.title: Natural Resources and Where They Are Found
versions.text:
The Earth provides a remarkably wide range of things that human societies rely upon every day, and these are consistently referred to as natural resources. Oil is one such resource, and water, minerals, and timber harvested from forests are resources as well, and modern economies depend upon all of them in countless, often invisible ways. Companies routinely dig or drill deep into the earth to extract many of these resources, sometimes descending several thousand meters below the surface in pursuit of them.

Not every region of the Earth possesses the same resources, and the disparity between regions can be genuinely enormous. Some countries find themselves sitting atop vast reserves of oil, whereas others possess almost none whatsoever. Some regions receive abundant rainfall throughout the year, whereas others remain persistently dry for most of it, a difference that directly affects how much fresh water is genuinely available to their populations.

Why, then, are natural resources distributed so unevenly across the entire planet? The answer lies predominantly in geology and climate. Hot, humid regions situated near the equator can sustain thick, dense rainforests, whereas arid desert regions simply cannot sustain one at all. Certain extraordinarily ancient layers of rock, formed over millions of years from the compressed remains of buried marine life, trap oil far underground, whereas comparatively younger rock may trap none whatsoever. Mineral deposits likewise form under their own distinct geologic conditions, frequently linked to ancient volcanic activity or to tectonic plates shifting deep within the planet's crust. Rivers, glaciers, and rainfall patterns, in turn, largely determine where fresh water naturally tends to accumulate.

Consequently, one country may possess abundant oil yet remarkably little fresh water, whereas a distant country may possess abundant water yet no oil reserves whatsoever. This profoundly uneven distribution constitutes a major reason why countries persistently trade resources with one another, continually exchanging what they hold in abundance for what they fundamentally lack.

Oil and minerals constitute finite resources, meaning their supply is inherently limited and will inevitably run out over time. In regions receiving comparatively little rainfall, fresh water can likewise become genuinely scarce, a circumstance that necessitates careful, long-term planning for the decades ahead.

MID.prompt: Explain why natural resources are distributed unevenly around the world. Use at least three details from the article.
checklist: I explained the role of geology.
I explained the role of climate.
I used at least two key words, such as distribute or deposit.
MID.modelAnswer: Natural resources are distributed unevenly around the world because of geology and climate. Ancient layers of rock, formed over millions of years, trap oil in some places but not others, and mineral deposits form only under certain geologic conditions. Climate matters too: hot, wet regions near the equator can support thick rainforests, while dry regions can not, and some places get far more rain and fresh water than others. Because of this uneven distribution, one country may have abundant oil but little water, so countries trade resources with each other.

keyWords.definition: not enough of something; hard to find or in short supply
keyWords.example: Clean drinking water is scarce in some desert regions.

keyWords.definition: to take something out, especially from the ground
keyWords.example: Workers extract copper from deep mines in the mountains.

keyWords.definition: an amount of a resource that is available and ready to be used
keyWords.example: The country has a large reserve of natural gas beneath its desert.

keyWords.definition: having a limit; not endless, and able to run out
keyWords.example: Fossil fuels are a finite resource, so they will not last forever.
Sunlight is abundant in most deserts, even though water is not.

questions.stem: Which statement best summarizes the article?
options: Gulf countries hold large oil reserves.
Rivers and glaciers shape where fresh water collects.
Mineral deposits form near ancient volcanoes.
Natural resources are distributed unevenly because of geology and climate, making some finite resources abundant in one country and scarce in another.
questions.why: The article's main point is that uneven geology and climate make finite resources abundant in some countries and scarce in others.

wrong.A: Gulf oil reserves are one example, not the whole idea.
wrong.B: Rivers and glaciers are one detail about water, not the central idea.
wrong.C: Volcanic mineral deposits are one detail, not the central idea.

questions.stem: What two forces does the article say mainly explain the uneven distribution of resources?
options: Trade and population
Government and economy
Geology and climate
Agriculture and industry
questions.why: The article says geology and climate mainly explain why resources are distributed unevenly.

wrong.A: Trade and population are effects of uneven resources, not the main causes.
wrong.B: Government and economy are not described as the main causes.
wrong.D: Agriculture and industry are not described as the main causes.

questions.stem: According to the article, what can form oil underground over millions of years?
options: Ancient layers of rock from buried sea life
Modern factories near the coast
Rainfall collecting in rivers
Minerals mixing with fresh water
questions.why: The article says certain ancient layers of rock, formed from buried sea life, trap oil underground.

wrong.B: Modern factories are not described as forming oil.
wrong.C: Rivers are linked to fresh water, not oil formation.
wrong.D: Minerals and fresh water are described separately from oil formation.

questions.stem: The article describes oil and minerals as finite resources. What does finite mean here?
options: Impossible to extract from the ground
Found only in hot desert climates
Having a limit and able to eventually run out
Traded only between two countries
questions.why: The article uses finite to describe resources with a limited supply that will eventually run out.

wrong.A: Being hard to extract is different from being finite.
wrong.B: Finite describes supply, not where a resource is found.
wrong.D: Finite describes supply, not how a resource is traded.

questions.stem: Why can fresh water become scarce in some regions, according to the article?
options: Because those regions have too many mineral deposits
Because those regions receive little rainfall
Because those regions trade too much oil
Because those regions have no tectonic plates
questions.why: The article links scarce fresh water to regions that receive little rainfall.

wrong.A: Mineral deposits are not linked to water scarcity.
wrong.C: Oil trade is not linked to water scarcity.
wrong.D: Tectonic plates are linked to mineral formation, not water scarcity.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about a country with an abundant oil reserve but very little fresh water?
options: It must have no climate at all
It will automatically develop thick rainforests
It may need to trade for water while exporting oil
It cannot use its oil reserve for anything
questions.why: The article suggests a country rich in oil but poor in water may trade its oil for water from elsewhere.

wrong.A: Every region has some kind of climate.
wrong.B: Rainforests need a hot, wet climate, not just oil wealth.
wrong.D: An oil reserve can still be used for trade even without water.

questions.stem: Why does the uneven distribution of finite resources encourage trade between countries?
options: Because every country has identical reserves of everything
Because finite resources can never actually be extracted
Because trade causes resources to regenerate instantly
Because one country's abundance can make up for another's scarcity
questions.why: The article suggests trade works because one country's abundance of a resource can offset another country's scarcity of it.

wrong.A: The article shows reserves differ between countries.
wrong.B: The article describes resources being extracted, not impossible to extract.
wrong.C: Finite resources do not regenerate just because they are traded.

questions.stem: How does the article compare oil-rich and water-rich countries?
options: It shows that no country can be rich in both oil and water
It shows that a country can be rich in oil but scarce in water, while another is the reverse
It shows that oil-rich countries always have abundant water too
It shows that water-rich countries never need oil
questions.why: The article compares countries, showing that one may be rich in oil but scarce in water, while another is the reverse.

wrong.A: The article describes countries rich in one resource but not another, not countries with both being impossible.
wrong.C: The article does not say oil-rich countries always have abundant water.
wrong.D: The article does not say water-rich countries never need oil.

HIGH.prompt: Is it fair that some countries have abundant natural resources while others have very few? Use evidence from the article to support your answer.
checklist: I used evidence about geology and climate from the article.
I used at least two key words, such as finite or abundant.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I think the uneven distribution of natural resources is not really a matter of fairness, because it comes from geology and climate, forces no country can control. Ancient rock formed from buried sea life trapped oil in some places over millions of years, while different climates made some regions wet enough for rainforests and left others scarce in fresh water. Because every country ends up with an abundant supply of some resources and a shortage of others, trade becomes a natural and necessary way to balance these finite resources fairly across the world.
